blocks.prompt: Read this out loud
blocks.text: A campfire starts small. We build it with sticks and logs. Soon the flames grow tall. They are orange and yellow. They wiggle up to the sky. The fire pops and snaps. That is water inside the wood turning to steam. The fire feels warm on your face. Sit back. Do not touch. When we go home, we pour water on it until every piece is cold.

blocks.prompt: What Is Really Burning
blocks.text: A campfire looks like it is burning the wood. It is not, or at least not the way you think. When wood gets very hot, it puffs out gas. The gas is what catches fire. So those tall orange flames are burning gas, and they float just above the sticks. Down at the bottom, the wood turns black and glows red. That part burns with almost no flame. A fire needs three things: wood to burn, air, and heat to start it. Take away any one of them and the fire goes out. Water works because it steals the heat away.

blocks.prompt: Why the Flames Point Up
blocks.text: Sit close to a campfire and your face gets warm while your back stays cold. That is a clue about how fire sends out heat. Some of the warmth rises away with the smoke and never reaches you at all. The rest travels in straight lines, like light does, until it hits something. It hits your face, so your face gets warm. Your back is turned away, so your back stays cool. Now watch the flames. They point up, even on a still night with no wind. Hot gas is lighter than cool air, so it floats upward, and fresh air gets pulled in from the sides to take its place. That upward rush is what stretches a flame into its pointy teardrop shape. Astronauts have lit tiny flames on the space station, where nothing is heavy and nothing floats up. Those flames were not pointy at all. They were small blue balls. The pops and snaps are simpler. Wood holds water and sticky sap. Heat turns them into steam, the pressure builds, and a little pocket bursts open.

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

blocks.prompt: The Flames Are Not Touching the Log
blocks.text: Watch a campfire long enough and a question shows up. If the log is what is burning, why do the flames float above it instead of sitting on it? The answer is that the log is not really what burns. Wood is a solid, and solids do not catch fire easily. What happens is that heat cooks the wood from the inside. Once the wood gets hot enough, it begins to break down and release gases and vapors, a little like steam escaping a kettle, except that these gases will burn. Those escaping gases are what ignite. The flames hover in the space just above the wood because that is exactly where the gas is. That also explains what gets left behind. After the gases have cooked out, what remains is char: dark, light, and almost pure carbon. Char does not make tall flames. It glows instead, because it burns right at its own surface where it meets the air. A fire that has burned down to orange coals is often hotter than it was when the flames were leaping, which is why cooks wait for the coals rather than the blaze. Even the color of a flame is a clue. Down at the base, where there is plenty of air, a flame burns blue. Higher up the air runs short and tiny specks of unburned carbon form. Those specks get so hot that they glow, and that glow is the warm yellow you recognize. The friendly color of a campfire is really soot, lit up like the wire in an old light bulb, on its way to becoming smoke.

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: Fuel, oxygen, heat: the fire triangle

blocks.prompt: Three Sides of a Fire
blocks.text: Every fire needs exactly three things, and it needs all three at once. It needs fuel, which is anything that will burn. It needs oxygen, which the air supplies. And it needs heat, enough to start the reaction and enough to keep it going. Firefighters draw these three as a triangle, because taking away any single side collapses the whole thing. Smothering a pan with a lid removes the oxygen. Cutting a firebreak removes the fuel. Pouring water on a campfire removes the heat, since turning water into steam soaks up an enormous amount of energy. Once you know the triangle, a lot of campfire advice stops sounding like superstition. Thin dry twigs light easily because they carry a huge surface area for very little weight, so heat reaches all of them at once. A thick green log resists lighting because most of the heat pouring into it goes toward boiling the water trapped inside instead of raising the wood to the temperature where it releases burnable gas. Stacking wood loosely beats packing it tight, because air has to reach every surface. A fire that smokes heavily and burns dull is usually starving for air, not for fuel. Fire also runs in stages, and the stages look different. First the wood dries. Then it heats until it starts breaking apart and giving off flammable gas, and that gas is what the bright flames are actually consuming. When the gas is spent, what is left is char, and char glows rather than flames. Cooks prefer that stage. Steady coals deliver even heat without the soot and flare of open flame. The end of the night matters more than the beginning. Ash is an excellent insulator, so a bed of coals hidden underneath it can stay hot enough to set dry leaves alight more than a day later. The standard method is to drown the fire, stir the ashes, and drown it again, then hold a hand close to check for warmth. A fire is not out simply because it has stopped looking like a fire.

6.title: The Campfire That Burns Old Sunlight
6.subtitle: A reading and science sheet for age 13
6.intro: Read the passage closely, then answer in full sentences. Cite the text directly where a question asks for evidence.

meta.templateLabel: The Campfire That Burns Old Sunlight

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: Wood stores energy captured from sunlight
Pyrolysis: hot wood breaks down into burnable gas
Glowing char burns at its own surface
Yellow flame is incandescent soot
In orbit, flames burn as slow blue spheres
Controlled fire is at least 300,000 years old

blocks.prompt: Old Sunlight: What a Campfire Is Actually Doing
blocks.text: Every campfire is a delayed reaction to sunlight. A tree spends decades pulling carbon dioxide out of the air, splitting it apart using energy borrowed from the sun, and locking that carbon into wood. Burning the wood runs the entire process backward in an afternoon. The carbon returns to the air, the water leaves as steam, and the sunlight the tree banked years ago comes back out as heat and light. When you hold your hands over the flames, you are warming them with an old summer. The fire itself is stranger than it looks. Wood does not burn the way you might assume, with oxygen attacking the solid directly. Heat wood past roughly three hundred degrees Celsius and it begins to decompose, a process called pyrolysis, releasing a fog of flammable gases and vapors. Those gases are what ignite. The tall orange flames dancing above a log are not touching the log at all. They are burning a cloud of gas that the log is exhaling. Once the gases are spent, what remains is char, nearly pure carbon, and char behaves differently. It glows red with almost no flame, because it reacts with oxygen directly at its surface. That is why the last hour of a campfire is quiet and hot rather than tall and bright. The color tells you what is happening. At the base of a flame, where gas mixes with plenty of air, combustion is efficient and the flame runs blue. Higher up, oxygen runs short, and unburned carbon clumps into microscopic soot particles. Those particles are heated to thousands of degrees, and hot solids glow. The warm yellow of a campfire is not really the gas. It is soot, briefly incandescent, on its way to becoming smoke. Flames point upward for a reason that has nothing to do with fire and everything to do with weight. Hot gas is less dense than the cool air around it, so it rises, and cooler air is drawn in underneath to replace it. That constant upward current stretches a flame into its familiar teardrop. Astronauts have lit small flames aboard the space station, where floating and falling lose their usual meaning. With no buoyancy to shape them, those flames formed slow blue spheres, burning outward in every direction at once. Humans have been managing this reaction for a very long time. Archaeologists find solid evidence of controlled fire at sites used at least three hundred thousand years ago, and a few older sites hint that the habit may be far more ancient. Fire changed almost everything about us. It made cold nights survivable, pushed predators back, hardened wooden tools, and above all it cooked food. Cooking breaks down tough fibers and starches before they ever reach the stomach, so a cooked meal delivers more usable energy for less chewing and less digesting. Some researchers argue that this extra energy is part of what allowed our ancestors to afford a brain as expensive as ours. So a campfire is a small, well behaved version of the oldest tool we have, and it deserves the respect that comes with that. Coals buried under ash can hold enough heat to restart a fire more than a day later, which is why the rule is to drown the fire, stir it, and drown it again until you can hold a hand near the ashes without flinching. The same reaction that fed us can, left alone in dry country, take a forest.
